e.t: This word refers to decency and modesty—conduct marked by a proper, restrained sense of what is fitting. It describes an outward manner that avoids shameful or attention-seeking behavior and shows respect for what is appropriate. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Timothy 2:9, and is rendered “modesty” there. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is clear: behaving with becoming restraint and dignity.

e.t: This word means “to read,” describing the act of taking in and understanding written words. It is a verb used when someone reads Scripture or another written message, and it can be rendered as “read,” “reading,” or “reads.” In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 32 times, showing regular use for reading written material rather than referring to a special kind of spiritual experience. Its precise force in a verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This Greek New Testament word describes someone as “sinless” or “without sin.” It presents the person as having no sin, making it a direct description of moral innocence. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, at John 8:7. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains clear: a person who is not guilty of sin.

d: To examine (a person on trial, a witness) judicially (frequently by the aid of torture).

e.t: This word means “to question,” describing the act of asking someone for information or examining an matter through questions. It presents questioning as an action rather than naming a person, place, or thing. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Acts 22. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the act of questioning. [p03:word:greek-nt:G0426:identity] [p03:word:greek-nt:G0426:occurrences]

d: (free from hurt or harm, hence) not offending, not causing offence, blameless.

e.t: This word describes being blameless and not giving offence. It refers to conduct that does not provide a legitimate cause for accusation or unnecessarily place a stumbling block before others. In the Greek New Testament, it appears three times, expressing a concern for living with a clear conscience and treating others carefully. Its exact emphasis in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

d: A ruler of angels, a superior angel, an archangel.

e.t: This word means “archangel,” identifying a heavenly being with that designation. It appears twice in the Greek New Testament: once in 1 Thessalonians 4:16 and once in Jude 1:9. The word itself identifies the being, while the surrounding passage supplies the specific significance in each occurrence. Its consistent rendering as “archangel” supports this straightforward meaning rather than a broader or unrelated sense.

This word describes something disagreeable or discordant—out of harmony rather than in agreement. It can characterize people, words, or positions that do not fit together peacefully or consistently. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 28:25, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its basic sense points to disharmony, opposition, or a lack of agreement, without by itself explaining the reason for that disagreement or judging every person involved.

d: (a) Babylon, the ancient city on the Euphrates, to which the people of Jerusalem, etc., were transported, (b) hence allegorically of Rome, from the point of view of the Christian people.

e.t: Babylon is the name “Babylon,” referring to the place or power identified by that name in the Greek New Testament. It appears twelve times in eleven verses, beginning in Matthew and continuing through Revelation. The word occurs in genealogical records, historical speech, a personal greeting, and Revelation’s prophetic passages. Its basic meaning remains a proper name rather than a general description or action; the surrounding verse determines what aspect of Babylon is being mentioned.

This word means “baptism,” referring to the practice named by that term. It appears four times in the Greek New Testament, in Mark, Colossians, and Hebrews. The word is used in discussions that include Mark 7:4, Colossians 2:12, Hebrews 6:2, and Hebrews 9:10. Its precise significance in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its basic meaning remains baptism.

e.t: This word means “be vexed” or “to be greatly disturbed,” describing a person who is deeply troubled or agitated. It functions as an expression of strong inner distress rather than a calm or minor concern. In the Greek New Testament, it appears twice, both times in Acts, showing a focused use rather than a broadly repeated term. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is clear: being seriously troubled or upset.

This word refers to an ordinance—an established order or ruling—and can also describe putting such an order into effect. It points to an arrangement that carries authority and is enacted rather than merely proposed. The word occurs twice in the Greek New Testament, in Acts 7:53 and Romans 13:2. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This Greek New Testament word means “different”: it points to something distinct from what has already been mentioned or from another thing being compared. It can describe difference in kind, quality, or arrangement, depending on the sentence, so the surrounding words determine its precise force. The word occurs four times in the Greek New Testament, with three occurrences in Hebrews and one in Romans. Its central idea remains simple: not the same, but different.

me: Verb, Aorist, Active, Indicative, first, Plural

e.t: This word means “to give in” or “to yield.” It describes relinquishing resistance rather than continuing to oppose someone or something. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Galatians 2:5. That single appearance does not provide enough context here to describe the specific situation, but the word’s central idea is clear: a person stops resisting and yields. Its meaning should therefore be understood as an action of concession or surrender in the sentence where it appears.

d: Elymas, the name of the sorcerer at Paphos.

e.t: Elymas is the personal name of a person mentioned in the Greek New Testament. It functions as a proper name rather than a general description, title, action, or quality. The name appears once in the Greek New Testament, in Acts 13:8, and the English translations represented here retain it as “Elymas.” The name itself identifies the individual; its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, which is not included here.

Unity means a state of being joined together as one rather than divided. This noun names oneness, togetherness, or agreement among people or things. In the Greek New Testament, it appears twice, both times in Ephesians 4, and is rendered “unity.” Its central idea is a shared condition of being one. The precise aspect of unity in either occurrence depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

d: To send away, send forth (a person qualified for a task).

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “to send out” or “to send out/away.” It describes directing someone or something away from a place or source, so its basic idea is movement caused by another’s sending. It occurs 13 times in the Greek New Testament. Depending on the sentence, it can describe sending people away, sending them out, or dispatching them to another location. The surrounding verse determines the specific situation, but the central meaning remains sending forth or away.

me: ADVerb or adverb and particle combined

e.t: This word means “out” or “outside,” describing a place beyond an interior or boundary. It can indicate movement from within to without, position in an outer place, or people who are outside. In some passages, it refers to an outsider rather than someone belonging within a particular group. It occurs 63 times in the Greek New Testament, so its precise force depends on the sentence: it may describe physical location, departure, or exclusion from an inner setting.

This word means “conversion,” referring to a turning or change in a person’s direction toward God. It names the change itself rather than describing a person, place, or action in progress. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 15:3. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains conversion: a turning that brings about a changed spiritual direction.

d: Erastus, steward of Corinth, a Christian.

e.t: Erastus is a personal name, referring to a man named Erastus rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek New Testament, the name appears three times, each time identifying a person: in Acts 19:22, Romans 16:23, and 2 Timothy 4:20. The name is consistently rendered “Erastus.” Its precise significance in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but the word itself functions simply as this person’s name.

d: Thankfulness, gratitude; giving of thanks, thanksgiving.

e.t: This word means thankfulness or an expression of thanks. It describes the grateful acknowledgment offered to God or to another person, and it can refer either to the attitude of gratitude or its spoken expression. In the New Testament, it is used 15 times, showing a recurring emphasis on gratitude in worship, prayer, speech, and response to blessing. Its central idea is thankful recognition rather than a mere polite phrase.

d: A class of priests who served for a stated number of days.

e.t: This word means “division.” It identifies a distinct portion or organized section within a larger arrangement, rather than the whole. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Luke 1:5–8. Its basic sense is therefore a separated group, share, or scheduled section, while the surrounding verse determines exactly what is being divided or assigned. The word itself points to an organized division, not necessarily to conflict or separation between people.

d: Herodias (died after A.D. 40), daughter of Aristobulus and granddaughter of Herod I, wife, first, of her uncle Herod, second, of his half-brother, her uncle Herod Antipas.

e.t: Herodias is a personal name—the name of a woman mentioned in the Greek New Testament. It does not describe an action, quality, or general idea; it identifies a particular person. The name occurs six times, in Matthew, Mark, and Luke, and is rendered consistently as “Herodias.” In some sentences, an apostrophe appears in English because the name is used to show possession, but the word itself remains the person’s name. Its precise significance in any individual passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This word refers to death—the end of physical life. It can describe death as a real event, the condition people face, or the power and consequence associated with dying, depending on the surrounding sentence. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 120 times, showing that death is a recurring subject across its teaching and narrative. Its basic meaning remains consistent, while each passage supplies the particular force, contrast, or promise connected with death.

This word refers to “healing”—the restoration of health or freedom from sickness. It can also describe healings as acts or results of being made well. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, in Luke and Acts. The word names healing itself rather than the person who heals, the method used, or a particular illness. Its precise force in a verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This word refers to an advocate or proclaimer—someone who speaks publicly on behalf of a person, message, or cause. It appears once in the Greek New Testament, in Acts 17:18. Its central idea is a person who announces or champions something before others. The precise force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary sense centers on public advocacy or proclamation rather than private conversation.

d: Cursing; a curse; a doomed one.

e.t: This word means “curse.” It refers to a spoken condemnation or a condition marked by being cursed. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs six times in five verses, including three occurrences in Galatians. Its meaning remains centered on the idea of a curse rather than a general hardship, difficulty, or unpleasant outcome. The surrounding passage determines whether the word emphasizes the pronouncement itself or the condition that results from it.

“Koum” means “stand up!” It is a direct command calling someone to rise. The word functions as an urgent spoken instruction rather than a description or title. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs only once, in Mark 5:41. Its exact force in that verse is understood most fully from the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is clear: a person is being told to get up.

me: Verb, Imperfect, Either middle or passive, Indicative, third, Singular

e.t: This word describes rolling around or wallowing. It portrays a person or creature moving about on the ground rather than standing or walking normally. As an action word, it focuses on the physical movement itself. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Mark 9:20, so its exact force there is understood from the surrounding verse and passage. Its central meaning remains the act of rolling or wallowing on the ground.

Frankincense is the meaning of this Greek New Testament word. It names a distinct substance rather than an action, quality, or person. The word occurs twice in the Greek New Testament, once in Matthew and once in Revelation, and both occurrences are rendered “frankincense.” Its precise significance in either passage depends on the surrounding verse text, but the lexical sense itself remains clear: frankincense.

me: ADVerb or adverb and particle combined

e.t: This word means “wisely,” describing an action or response carried out with good judgment. It focuses on the manner in which someone acts rather than naming a person, object, or event. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Mark 12:34. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text and context, but its basic meaning is straightforward: acting or responding wisely.

This word describes someone who is compassionate and merciful—showing tender concern toward others and responding with mercy rather than harshness. It presents mercy as a quality of character, not merely an occasional action. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, in two verses, including Jesus’ call for his disciples to be merciful and James’s description of the Lord’s compassionate character. The ordinary sense is a person moved by compassion and ready to extend mercy.

d: By no means, not at all.
me: ADVerb or adverb and particle combined

e.t: This word means “by no means,” expressing a firm or emphatic denial. It is used when something is completely rejected rather than merely questioned or made unlikely. In ordinary English, it can correspond to a strong “certainly not” or “not at all,” while retaining the central idea of absolute refusal or denial. This Greek New Testament word occurs once, in Matthew 2:6. Its exact force in that verse is understood from the surrounding sentence, but its basic function is a decisive negative answer or rejection.

This word means “comfort.” It refers to bringing relief, consolation, or encouragement to someone who needs support. Its basic sense is personal and strengthening: it describes help that eases distress and gives renewed courage. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Colossians 4:11. The surrounding verse determines the precise emphasis there, but the word itself points to comfort offered to another person. It is therefore a word of supportive care rather than a description of an object, place, or event.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “to pass by.” It describes something moving past or going by, rather than remaining in place. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in Acts 14:16. Since the surrounding verse text is not included here, its safest ordinary meaning is movement beyond a place or time. Its precise force in that sentence depends on the surrounding context, but the central idea remains that something has passed along or gone beyond.

me: Verb, Present, Active, Indicative, third, Singular

e.t: This Greek New Testament verb means “to drive” someone into an irrational or disturbed state—to “drive insane.” It describes an action that causes a person to lose sound judgment or behave as though mentally unwell. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, at Acts 26:24. Its basic meaning identifies the effect produced on a person, while the surrounding verse determines exactly how that effect is expressed in context.

e.t: This word means “to advance” or “to go on,” expressing movement forward from one point to another. It describes someone proceeding or moving ahead rather than remaining in place. The word occurs five times in the Greek New Testament, appearing in Matthew, Mark, and Luke. Its exact force in any individual verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains forward movement or progress.

This word refers to “anticipation” or “expectation”—looking ahead toward what is expected to happen. It names the forward-looking attitude itself rather than the later result. In the Greek New Testament, it appears twice, in Luke and Acts, and it is rendered “expectation” in both occurrences. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains the act or state of awaiting what lies ahead.

Salim is a proper name, rendered “Salim.” It does not describe an action, quality, or general idea; it identifies a named person or place in the Greek New Testament. This name occurs once in the Greek New Testament, at John 3:23. The available lexical information preserves the name itself rather than giving a separate descriptive definition, so its precise referent is determined by the surrounding verse and passage.

d: To be bowed together, bent double.
me: Verb, Present, Active, Participle, Nominative, Singular, Feminine

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “to bend” or “to bend over.” It describes the act of curving downward rather than remaining upright. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in Luke 13:11. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is the physical action of bending or stooping. It functions as an action word, describing what someone does rather than naming a person, object, or quality.

d: To lead away with, carry along with (in good or bad sense according to context); to conform oneself willingly to.

Verb, Present, Middle, Participle, Nominative, Plural, Masculine

e.t: This word means “to be led away” or “to lead away with.” It describes someone being directed or drawn away, either alone or together with others. Its focus is the action or influence that causes a person to go along. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, in Romans 12:16, Galatians 2:13, and 2 Peter 3:17. Its precise force in each passage depends on the surrounding sentence and argument.

Conscience refers to a person’s inward moral awareness, especially the inner sense that evaluates whether one’s conduct is right or wrong. In the Greek New Testament, it is consistently rendered “conscience,” with the plural “consciences” appearing as well. The word occurs 30 times in 29 verses, making it a recurring term for describing a person’s moral awareness rather than a rare or specialized idea.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “to be buried with” or “be buried with.” It describes being joined with someone in burial, expressed as an action rather than simply naming a burial. The word occurs twice in the Greek New Testament, once in Romans and once in Colossians. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and argument, but its central idea remains shared burial or being placed in burial together with another.

d: To be more than conqueror, prevail mightily.
me: Verb, Present, Active, Indicative, first, Plural

e.t: This word means to conquer, especially to conquer thoroughly or completely. It describes decisive victory rather than merely enduring or escaping defeat. As a verb, it can express the action of overcoming in a powerful, comprehensive way. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Romans 8:37. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text, but its central idea is clear: successful victory over opposition.

This word describes something green, including a light-green color. It is a color term used for things that appear fresh or verdant, such as vegetation or other visibly green objects. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs four times, appearing once in Mark and three times in Revelation. Its exact reference depends on the noun it describes, but its central meaning remains the same: green or light green.

d: To help, benefit, do good, to be useful (to), profit.

e.t: This word means to help, benefit, or be of good use. It describes something that provides real advantage or assistance, especially when the question is whether an action, possession, or circumstance truly benefits someone. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 15 times, expressing the idea of usefulness or help rather than merely describing an object or activity. Its exact force in any sentence depends on what the surrounding passage identifies as helpful or beneficial.

This word means “accuser”: someone who charges another with wrongdoing. It functions as a noun, identifying a person who brings an accusation against someone else. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Revelation 12:10, and is rendered “accuser.” The word’s basic meaning is therefore a person who makes accusations, while the surrounding verse determines the specific force of that accusation. Its one occurrence does not by itself establish a broader range of meanings.
